prompt: Many countries invest heavily in training doctors, engineers and other skilled professionals, only for large numbers of them to emigrate soon after qualifying. Why does this happen, and what measures could reduce it?
essay:
It is a painful arithmetic for a poorer country: the state pays to train a surgeon over a decade, and a wealthier health service acquires the finished professional at no cost at all. Understanding why this happens matters more than deploring it, because the reasons point directly at what might be changed.

The obvious driver is income. A specialist can often earn several times more abroad, and the difference is large enough that no realistic domestic pay rise would close it. But money alone explains less than it appears to. Surveys of emigrating professionals consistently place working conditions, career progression and the ability to practise properly alongside salary, and often above it. A doctor who cannot obtain basic supplies is not only underpaid; they are prevented from doing the job they trained for, which is a different and in some ways more corrosive frustration.

This suggests that the more promising measures are not financial at all. Investment in the equipment, staffing and management that allow professionals to work effectively addresses the frustration directly, and it does so at a cost far below matching foreign salaries. Clear promotion structures matter for the same reason: much emigration occurs when a capable person can see no path upward at home.

Bonded service agreements, in which graduates repay subsidised training through a period of domestic work, have a place, but a limited one. They can recover the public investment, and they may retain someone long enough for circumstances to improve. What they cannot do is make a frustrating job satisfying, and a professional who is compelled to stay is not necessarily a professional who works well.
title: When trained graduates leave the country that educated them
